summary.title: The structural basis for regulation of the glutathione transporter Ycf1 by regulatory domain phosphorylation
summary.authors: Nitesh Kumar Khandelwal; Cinthia R Millan; Samantha I Zangari; Samantha Avila; Dewight Williams; Tarjani M Thaker; Thomas M Tomasiak
summary.executive_summary: This study presents the first high-resolution cryo-EM structures of the yeast glutathione transporter Ycf1, revealing the structural basis for its regulation by phosphorylation. Ycf1, an ABCC transporter, sequesters heavy metals and oxidized glutathione into the vacuole to protect cells from stress. While phosphorylation is known to regulate many ABC transporters, the mechanism remains poorly understood due to the intrinsic disorder of their regulatory domains (R-domains). Here, the authors report two inward-facing conformations of Ycf1 at 3.4 Å and 4.0 Å resolution, capturing a previously unobserved ordered state of the R-domain. The structures show that the R-domain is phosphorylated at three sites (S908, T911, S914) and forms extensive electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with Nucleotide Binding Domain 1 (NBD1) and the lasso domain. These interactions are conserved between the wide and narrow inward-facing states, which are related by rigid body movements of the NBD1/R-domain complex. Biochemical assays demonstrate that dephosphorylation of the R-domain significantly reduces ATPase activity and alters the protein's proteolytic profile, indicating that phosphorylation stabilizes an active architecture. The study challenges previous models suggesting that phosphorylation releases the R-domain into a disordered state, instead proposing that phosphorylation drives the R-domain to bind NBD1, stabilizing the transporter in a primed, active conformation. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how post-translational modifications regulate ABCC transporters and offer insights into related human diseases like cystic fibrosis.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents the first high-resolution cryo-EM structures of the yeast glutathione transporter Ycf1, revealing the structural basis for its regulation by phosphorylation. Ycf1, an ABCC transporter, sequesters heavy metals and oxidized glutathione into the vacuole to protect cells from stress. While phosphorylation is known to regulate many ABC transporters, the mechanism remains poorly understood due to the intrinsic disorder of their regulatory domains (R-domains). Here, the authors report two inward-facing conformations of Ycf1 at 3.4 Å and 4.0 Å resolution, capturing a previously unobserved ordered state of the R-domain. The structures show that the R-domain is phosphorylated at three sites (S908, T911, S914) and forms extensive electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with Nucleotide Binding Domain 1 (NBD1) and the lasso domain. These interactions are conserved between the wide and narrow inward-facing states, which are related by rigid body movements of the NBD1/R-domain complex. Biochemical assays demonstrate that dephosphorylation of the R-domain significantly reduces ATPase activity and alters the protein's proteolytic profile, indicating that phosphorylation stabilizes an active architecture. The study challenges previous models suggesting that phosphorylation releases the R-domain into a disordered state, instead proposing that phosphorylation drives the R-domain to bind NBD1, stabilizing the transporter in a primed, active conformation. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how post-translational modifications regulate ABCC transporters and offer insights into related human diseases like cystic fibrosis.

Research Context
Ycf1 transports glutathione and heavy metals into vacuoles to counter cell stress. Ycf1 belongs to the ABCC subfamily of ATP-binding cassette transporters. Many ABCC transporters are regulated by phosphorylation on intrinsically disordered domains. The regulatory mechanism of phosphorylation in these transporters is poorly understood. Previous cryo-EM structures of ABCC transporters showed mostly disordered R-domains. Lack of sequence assignment in previous models limited understanding of R-domain interactions. No structure of an intact R-domain with NBDs had been determined previously.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to determine how R-domain phosphorylation regulates Ycf1 activity. The authors hypothesize that phosphorylation induces structural changes in the R-domain. They predict that these structural changes affect ATPase activity. The study seeks to resolve the ordered state of the R-domain. The hypothesis is that phosphorylation stabilizes interactions between the R-domain and NBD1. The authors propose that this stabilization is required for maximal ATPase activity.

Methodological Details
Ycf1 was expressed in S. cerevisiae DSY5 strain. Two forms were purified: wild-type (WT) and NBD2 Walker B mutant E1435Q. Cryo-EM grids were prepared for both WT and E1435Q Ycf1 in apo conditions. Only the E1435Q dataset yielded homogenous particles for structure determination. Two inward-facing conformations were identified: IFwide and IFnarrow. The E1435Q mutant had substantially lowered ATPase activity compared to WT. Data processing was performed using RELION and cisTEM. Model building was guided by evolutionary coupling analysis. ATPase assays were conducted using an enzyme-coupled assay. Phosphorylation was characterized using mass spectrometry and phosphostaining.

Procedures And Architectures
The Ycf1 gene was codon-optimized and cloned into a yeast expression vector. Protein expression was induced by adding YPG media. Purification involved lysis, affinity chromatography, and size exclusion chromatography. Cryo-EM data was processed with drift correction and CTF estimation. Particle picking was performed manually and automatically using reference maps. 3D classification and refinement were performed in RELION. The final structures were refined using Phenix and CCP-EM modules. Evolutionary coupling analysis used 13,723 sequences from Uniref90. ATPase rates were determined at 30°C using NADH consumption monitoring. Dephosphorylated Ycf1 was generated using lambda phosphatase treatment.

Key Results
Two cryo-EM structures of Ycf1 were determined at 3.4 Å and 4.0 Å resolution. The structures captured an ordered state of the intrinsically disordered R-domain. R-domain phosphorylation was observed at S908, T911, and S914. Phosphorylation induced electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with NBD1 and the lasso domain. These interactions were constant between the IFwide and IFnarrow states. Dephosphorylation of Ycf1 resulted in a drastic reduction in ATPase activity. Dephosphorylated Ycf1 showed increased protease accessibility in limited proteolysis assays. The R-domain buried ~1530 Å² and ~1338 Å² of surface area in IFnarrow and IFwide, respectively. The IFnarrow state showed occlusion of the non-functional ATP binding site in NBD1. GSSG stimulated ATPase activity at physiologically relevant concentrations.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The findings challenge the model where phosphorylation releases the R-domain into a disordered state. Instead, phosphorylation drives the R-domain to bind NBD1, stabilizing an active architecture. This stabilization is required for maximal ATPase activity. The R-domain acts as a regulatory "clutch" that engages the motor without performing work. The structures provide a plausible explanation for the inhibitory role of S251 phosphorylation. These insights may inform the development of allosteric modulators for ABCC transporters.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study does not rule out an inhibitory role for the unphosphorylated state. The NBD2 region was less ordered, limiting detailed modeling in some states. A third state, IFtransition, was insufficiently detailed for model building. The study focuses on Ycf1, so generalizability to other ABCC transporters requires further validation. The exact mechanism of how phosphorylation prevents protease accessibility is not fully resolved.

Claims
R-domain phosphorylation stabilizes an active conformation of Ycf1 required for maximal ATPase activity. Dephosphorylation drastically reduced ATPase activity. Phosphorylated R-domain formed extensive contacts with NBD1. Phosphorylation increased protease resistance. The unphosphorylated state may still have some activity. This mechanism may apply to other ABCC transporters.
The R-domain is ordered and bound to NBD1 in the phosphorylated state, contrary to previous models. Cryo-EM structures showed an ordered R-domain. Phosphorylation sites were resolved in the structure. Previous structures showed disordered R-domains. This provides a new model for ABCC regulation.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The E1435Q mutant was used to trap inward-facing conformations. Dephosphorylation experiments confirmed the functional role of phosphorylation. Evolutionary coupling analysis supported the R-domain/NBD1 interaction interface.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the cryo-EM structures of IFwide and IFnarrow states. Figure 2 details the R-domain phosphorylation and interactions. Figure 3 illustrates the hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions stabilizing the R-domain. Figure 4 compares the NBD orientation in IFwide and IFnarrow states.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first high-resolution structures of Ycf1 with an ordered, phosphorylated R-domain. 2. The strongest evidence is the correlation between R-domain phosphorylation, structural stability, and ATPase activity. 3. The future path involves applying these insights to understand and modulate other ABCC transporters.
